title: Purim: turned upside down (Esther 9:1)
hook: on the very day meant for destruction, everything is reversed
tomorrow: Purim: two gifts to the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Fast of Esther. Your line was before the feast, a fast. Did your one small fast get you ready for something? Tonight the fast breaks, and the feast is Purim. Day six hundred seventy-three.

Haman, the king's chief minister, wants every Jew in the empire dead. To choose the day, he casts lots, and the lot falls on the thirteenth of Adar, nearly a year away. That lot, in Hebrew pur, gives the holiday its name: Purim, lots. The book of Esther is full of plans that go exactly the wrong way for the person making them. Haman builds a tall gallows for Mordecai. Haman walks into the palace expecting honor and ends up leading Mordecai through the streets on the king's horse, shouting his praises. And by chapter nine, the book has a two-word Hebrew phrase for all of it.
screen: `PUR: A LOT CAST FOR A DAY.` → `A GALLOWS BUILT FOR MORDECAI.` → `HAMAN LEADS THE HORSE.`

segments.voice: Chapter nine opens on the thirteenth of Adar itself, the day Haman chose. The enemies of the Jews had hoped, the text says, to rule over them. And then: v'nahafoch hu. It was turned around. Upside down. Instead, the Jews ruled over those who hated them. The phrase is short, and in Hebrew it's almost a shrug: and it turned over. The root, h-f-ch, is the one used for overturning, the way you'd flip a cup or turn a coat inside out. It's the hinge of the whole book. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built. Mordecai wears the royal robes Haman wanted for himself. The day of destruction becomes a day of rescue, and the month of grief, the book says a few verses later, becomes a month of gladness. The Talmud adds a reversal of its own. In tractate Megillah, it says Haman was delighted when the lot fell in Adar, because Moses died in Adar. What he didn't know, the Talmud says, is that Moses was also born in Adar. Purim takes this idea and turns it into how the day feels. People wear costumes and become someone else. Synagogues fill with noisemakers. Children dress as kings and queens. Some communities appoint a Purim rabbi who makes fun of the real one. The Talmud even says one should drink on Purim until one can't tell cursed is Haman from blessed is Mordecai, a line rabbis have debated ever since, and many say means much less than it sounds. Purim is a holiday where the world, for a day, is allowed to stand on its head, because once, on a very bad day, it did.
screen: `THE DAY HAMAN CHOSE.` · `V'NAHAFOCH HU: IT TURNED OVER.` · `HANGED ON HIS OWN GALLOWS.` · `BORN AND DIED IN ADAR.` · then, large: `TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find something that turned for the better. Settle, and breathe. Go back over the last few years, and find one moment that looked like a disaster when it happened: a rejection, a move, a door that closed, a plan that fell apart. Then trace what came after. What grew out of it that you wouldn't give back? You don't have to call it a miracle. Just notice the turn. Stay with it. The bell holds the time.
V'nahafoch hu. It was turned upside down: the hinge of the book of Esther, and the feeling of Purim. Today's word.
Your line: turned upside down. Today, when something goes wrong, say it once to yourself, and wait to see which way it turns. Day six hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: On Purim, the fourteenth of Adar (the fifteenth in walled cities like Jerusalem), Jews hear the book of Esther read aloud at night and in the morning, making noise at Haman's name, and many wear costumes and hold a festive meal.

fork.setup: you're Haman. the king asks what should be done for the man he wants to honor. you're sure he means you. what do you suggest?
options: royal robes, the king's horse, and a herald.
a seat at the king's right hand.
fork.reveal: Haman asks for the royal robes, the king's horse and a herald, and then has to give them all to Mordecai. the first reversal.

original.note: Hebrew: and it was turned over. from Esther 9:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: Purim is a costume party.
what it means: the day of destruction turned into rescue, and the holiday turns the world over to remember it.
what a scholar hears: v'nahafoch hu in Esther 9:1, the root of overturning, and a book built of reversals; Megillah 13b's Adar teaching.

notes: Esther 9:1 paraphrased rather than quoted, as the exact JPS 1917 wording ('whereas it was turned to the contrary') could not be confirmed.
Lots cast in Nisan for a day in Adar (3:7); described as 'nearly a year away'. Verify.
Megillah 13b: Haman rejoiced that the lot fell in the month Moses died, not knowing he was also born then (7 Adar). Verify.
Megillah 7b: 'ad d'lo yada' (drink until one cannot distinguish); interpretations vary widely; presented without endorsing heavy drinking.
